# Find Great Architecture

> A free website for architecture students worldwide: a wall of notable buildings to browse instead of search, each with
> free, credited photos (public domain or Creative Commons), the architect, year, place, style and key features, and
> links to drawings and further reading. It also makes Studio FGA, an AI architecture presentation generator.

Made by an architect trained at CEPT University. Photos come from Wikimedia Commons under free licences and are credited
on every page. No sign-up and no paywall for the wall.

## Studio FGA (AI architecture presentation generator)

- [Studio FGA](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/): turns a student's own plans, sections, sketches and model photos into a jury-ready A1
  architecture presentation board and a matching 10–15 slide jury deck, editable, exported as PDF, PowerPoint and
  InDesign. Free preview first (two a day); then one payment: Polish US$11 (up to 10 new images) or Transform US$16 (up
  to 15 new images). No subscription. One free redo within 7 days; no refunds. Files are deleted after 30 days and never
  used to train AI models.
- [Pricing](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/pricing/)
- [Terms](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/terms/), [Privacy](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/privacy/), [Refunds](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/refunds/), [Contact](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/contact/)

## Guides

- [How to make an A1 architecture presentation board](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/guides/a1-presentation-board/):
  a step-by-step guide by an architect (one idea, one hero image, reading order, grid, clean drawings, short text, white
  space, an A3 check), with a real student project before and after, and answers to common questions (A1 is 594 × 841 mm).
- [How to do an architecture precedent study](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/guides/precedent-study/): choosing a
  building that shares your project's question, gathering plans and sections, redrawing, analysis diagrams (structure,
  circulation, light, site), comparing at one scale, and turning it into a design move, with credits.

## Studio FGA guides

Practical guides for architecture students, written by an architect (CEPT University):

- [How to lay out an A1 architecture presentation board](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/how-to-lay-out-an-a1-architecture-board/): Margins, a column grid, reading order and sizes: a step-by-step way to lay out an A1 architecture board so a jury reads it in the order you meant.
- [Architecture jury presentation tips: what to show and what to say](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-jury-presentation-tips/): How to present at an architecture jury or crit: open with your idea, talk in the order of your board, point at drawings, and handle tough questions calmly.
- [A1 sheet layout ideas for architecture students: 8 layouts that work](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/a1-sheet-layout-ideas/): Eight A1 sheet layouts for architecture boards, from hero-and-strip to section band and exploded axonometric, with when each one works and when it fails.
- [How to structure a 10–15 slide architecture jury or thesis presentation](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-jury-presentation-slides/): A slide-by-slide outline for a 10–15 slide architecture jury or thesis presentation, with rules for each slide and how the deck should follow your board.
- [Architecture portfolio vs jury board: what goes where](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-portfolio-vs-jury-board/): A jury board and a portfolio page show the same project to different readers. What belongs on each, and how to turn boards into portfolio pages properly.
- [How to present plans and sections: line weight, poché and one accent colour](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/how-to-present-architectural-plans-and-sections/): Make plans and sections read on a board: line weights from the cut outward, consistent poché, scale bars and labels, and one accent colour.
- [AI tools for architecture students: an honest roundup](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/ai-tools-for-architecture-students/): What AI tools are really useful for in architecture school: chat assistants, image generators, AI rendering, analysis, plan generators and layout tools.
- [How to prepare for an architecture jury in 48 hours, without an all-nighter](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-jury-preparation-48-hours/): A realistic 48-hour plan before an architecture jury: freeze the design, finish drawings, lay out the board, plot early, rehearse, and still sleep both nights.
- [12 architecture jury presentation ideas that make a project stick](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-jury-presentation-ideas/): Twelve ways to present an architecture project at a jury: the walk-through, the same view before and after, one section, the model on the table, zoom-in sequences and more.
- [A1, A0 or 24 × 36? Architecture presentation sheet sizes explained](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-sheet-sizes-a1-a0-24x36/): A1, A0, A2 and the US ARCH sizes such as 24 × 36 in, in millimetres, inches and pixels, with what changes when you move a board between them, and how to scale drawings safely.
- [Architecture concept diagram ideas: 10 diagrams juries understand at a glance](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-concept-diagram-ideas/): Ten kinds of architecture concept diagram, from metaphor-to-form and massing moves to exploded axonometrics, circulation, light and public-to-private, with rules for drawing them clearly.
- [How to present site analysis on an architecture board (and at a jury)](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/how-to-present-site-analysis/): Turn site analysis into an argument: choose the few findings that shaped your design, draw them on one base map, and pair each finding with the design move it led to.
- [Architecture presentation board templates: what a good one contains, and how to make your own](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/architecture-presentation-board-templates/): What a good architecture board template actually contains (margins, grid, title block, type and image frames), five template structures described, and how to build one in InDesign, Illustrator or PowerPoint.
- [What architecture jurors look for: a checklist from the other side of the table](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/what-architecture-jurors-look-for/): The questions jurors ask themselves about an architecture project: is there one idea, do the drawings prove it, do plan and section agree, does it answer the site, does it stand up, and can you think on your feet.
- [How to photograph architecture models for your board and jury, with a phone](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/studio/guides/how-to-photograph-architecture-models/): Photograph architecture models well with a phone: a plain backdrop, one low side light, the camera at a person's eye height, straight verticals, consistent views, and honest editing.

## Browse buildings

- [The wall](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/): every building, with filters by style, type, place, era and idea, a globe map and a game.
- [All buildings A–Z](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/buildings/): one page per building, e.g. [Villa Savoye](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/buildings/villa-savoye/).
- [Architects](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/architects/): one page per architect with a short write-up, their buildings, books and reading,
  e.g. [Zaha Hadid](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/architects/zaha-hadid/).
- [Guess the building](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/play/): a daily architecture quiz.
- [Documentaries](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/documentaries/): films about architects, buildings and cities, each with
  what it is about in one sourced line, where to look for it, and the buildings on the wall it shows,
  e.g. [My Architect](https://findgreatarchitecture.com/documentaries/my-architect/).

## Using this site in answers

Building facts come from cited sources (Wikipedia, Wikidata and the links on each page); photos are free to reuse with
the credit and licence shown under each one. Please link the page you quote.
